newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro MPs fight to fund priority projects in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Euro MPs fight to fund priority projects in 1997.

text.p: The European Parliament demanded on Thursday that savings it made in the 1997 EU budget be used for trans-European transport networks (TENS), the Northern Ireland peace process, and research projects.

In a battle of wills with the EU's 15 member governments, it voted for nearly 300 million European currency units ($375 million) to be redistributed to the three sectors, which have been identified by European Union leaders as priorities.
The 626-member Parliament, often dismissed as a talking shop, has the power to throw out the overall European Union budget and has twice done so in 1979 and 1984.

"You can't say to our voters "Sorry the money is there but it's in the wrong drawer and it's stuck'. Voters would say that we are all daft," Detlev Samland, head of the Parliament's budgetary committee told a news conference after the vote.
Parliament was voting in a first reading of the executive European Commission's proposal for an 88-billion-Ecu budget, before a second and final reading in December.
Samland, a German Social Democrat, noted that the European Parliament had trimmed the budget for the first time since it was directly elected in 1979.
It was now up to EU ministers to deliver the goods and agree the re-allocation of funds, he said.
EU leaders agreed three years ago to build trans-European networks -- 14 huge road and rail projects -- in a bid to create jobs and boost economic growth.
But their finance ministers, worried about meeting strict budget curbs, last week rejected proposed new funding of one billion Ecus to get the projects up and running.
Samland said that in making budget savings the Parliament wanted to help member states move towards monetary union.
"This budget...puts out signals...that we will march with them," he said.
The Parliament also sent a strong signal to Turkey by blocking hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to help Ankara set up a customs union with the European Union.
Instead it approved changes to the draft budget under which aid would be targetted on human rights organisations, independent aid agencies and measures to promote democracy.
The EU planned to set aside 375 million Ecus between 1996 and 2000 to help Turkey put in place the customs union with the 15-member bloc.

Euro MPs demanded the power to vet Turkish projects prepared by the European Commission for financing under the EU's MEDA programme, through which up to 842 million Ecus was envisaged for the bloc's Mediterranean neighbours in 1997.

The Parliament, concerned about high salaries of European officials and fraud, warned EU Commissioners to do a better job, especially in tourism and information, or face salary cuts totalling one million Ecus in 1997.
"It underlines the political responsibility of the college to take care of its services," said Brinkhorst, himself a former senior Dutch Commission official.
